paper_title: Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-Uni: Elastic Self-Refining Unified Diffusion LLM with Cross-Paradigm On-Policy Distillation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We propose Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-Uni (NLD-Uni), a unified discrete diffusion large language model (DLLM) for visual understanding and generation tasks. Compared with prior unified diffusion models, NLD-Uni introduces two major innovations. First, we propose a unified cross-paradigm on-policy distillation (OPD) framework that successfully transfers the visual understanding ability of autoregressive VLMs and visual generation ability of continuous flow models, to a unified DLLM. Second, NLD-Uni incorporates a novel progressive self-refining diffusion process that gradually corrupts each token across multiple steps during training, as opposed to adopting the conventional masked diffusion formulation that directly corrupts a clean image token to an uninformative mask token. At inference, this design allows NLD-Uni to make intermediate commit to a token, enabling progressive self-refinement for better visual quality. Through extensive experiments, we show that NLD-Uni achieves state-of-the-art performance among unified DLLMs on diverse tasks including visual question-answering, multi-modal reasoning, object grounding, text-to-image generation, and image editing.

Introduction Unified Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) [1, 2, 3, 4] have achieved strong performance on diverse multimodal understanding and generation tasks. Compared with specialist models, they learn to perform diverse tasks via unified sequence modeling interface, allowing synergetic learning that benefits each individual tasks [5]. They generally fall into two categories. The first design represents text and image as discrete tokens and employs unified autoregressive (AR) modeling paradigm [6, 4, 7]. The second design combines autoregressive modeling for text generation and continuous diffusion for image generation (AR+Diff) [5, 8, 9, 10]. Several recent works such as LaViDa-O [11] and MMaDA [12] explored third alternative that 2026 NVIDIA. All rights reserved. The VLM view uses the 8B understanding branch; the T2I view combines 4B understanding parameters with the 8B generation branch; and the interleaved view uses both full branches (16B). Each view loads only the parameters needed for its task. Representative examples demonstrate visual reasoning, object grounding, text-to-image synthesis, and image editing guided by reasoning and localization. builds unified discrete diffusion language model (unified DLLM) with masked diffusion paradigm (MDM). Unlike AR models or continuous flow models, MDMs randomly mask discrete tokens in sequence and learn to predict the masked tokens during training. At inference, MDMs initialize fully masked sequence and gradually unmask tokens across multiple diffusion steps. Compared with AR models, MDMs offer faster inference speed because they can generate multiple tokens in parallel [13, 14]. Compared with AR+Diff setup, which needs to carefully balance conflicting AR and Diffusion objectives [5], unified DLLMs offer single objective for both text and image, resulting in simplicity and, more importantly, scalability. Despite these advantages, substantial performance gap remains between existing unified DLLMs and domain-specialized VLMs and continuous flow models [12, 11]. In this work, we seek to narrow these gaps by introducing NLD-Uni, unified DLLM featuring new training paradigm and new architecture. First, although on-policy distillation (OPD) has proven highly effective in improving the visual understanding capabilities of VLMs [15] and the visual generation capabilities of continuous flow models [16], adapting it to unified MDMs is challenging because of lack of strong-performing MDM teachers. Distilling from strong AR VLMs and continuous flow models is not feasible because they follow fundamentally different paradigms. To overcome this challenge, we propose cross-paradigm on-policy distillation (OPD), which enables NLD-Uni to learn from teachers with different generation paradigms, including an AR VLM teacher for visual understanding and continuous flow teacher for visual generation. Second, for visual generation tasks specifically, MDMs lack the self-refinement capabilities of continuous flow models. At inference, each token jumps directly from masked state to clean state and stays unchanged afterwards. Since MDMs sample tokens independently from per-token logit prediction, all tokens sampled at the same diffusion step are assumed to be conditionally independent. This assumption rarely holds in practice since tokens from the same image are highly correlated. To address this limitation and enable iterative refinement, we introduce self-refining masked diffusion process that incorporates new intermediate 2 Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-Uni: Elastic Self-Refining Unified Diffusion LLM with Cross-Paradigm On-Policy Distillation states between the clean state and mask state. By breaking down the one-step jump to multi-step transition, NLD-Uni enables fine-grained inter-token interaction and progressive self-correction, resulting in better visual quality. To evaluate the effectiveness of NLD-Uni, we conduct extensive evaluations on diverse range of multimodal understanding and generation tasks, including visual question answering, object grounding, multimodal reasoning, text-to-image generation, and image editing. Experiments show that NLD-Uni achieves state-of-theart performance among unified DLLMs and greatly reduces the gap to specialized AR VLMs and continuous flow models. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: 1) We develop cross-paradigm OPD framework that improves both visual understanding and generation by distilling knowledge from non-DLLM teachers. 2) We introduce self-refining masked diffusion process that improves visual generation quality over the canonical masked diffusion process. 3) We present NLD-Uni, state-of-the-art unified DLLM capable of both understanding and generating visual content. We acknowledge that while extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our proposed methods, the model can be further improved via better data mixture and architecture optimization. 2. Preliminaries and Related Works 2.1. Diffusion Language Models Discrete diffusion language models [17, 13, 18] generate multiple text tokens in parallel, making them more efficient than AR models. However, its bidirectional attention introduces overhead compared to causal attention in AR models, particular for long sequences. Several works [19, 20] address this limitation through block-wise semi-auto-regressive generation. Notably, SBD [21, 22] incorporates variable-sized blocks during training, enabling flexible inference. Masked Discrete Image Models Masked image models generate images by initializing fully-masked image and gradually unmasking image patches. Each patch is encoded to discrete code through vector quantization (VQ) [23]. MaskGiT [24] pioneered this paradigm. Messonic [25] scaled it to large-scale T2I. Recent works such as LaViDa-O and MMaDa [11, 12] explored integrating masked image modeling to unified MLLMs. As discussed in Sec. 1, these models lack the self-refinement capabilities of continuous flow models. Some work mitigate this problem using specialized unmasking schedule that prioritizes unmasking less-correlated tokens [26, 11]. Others explored revising already unmasked [27, 28]. However, these works are sensitive to heuristic-based confidence thresholds and still present mismatch between training and inference setup. 2.3. On-Policy Distillation (OPD) OPD [29, 30] enables capability transfers from teacher model to student model by providing teacher supervision signals on student-generated sequences. M-OPD [31] extends OPD to multi-teacher setting to consolidate the capabilities of domain-specific experts. OPDLM [34] is the most relevant work, but its scope is limited to same-model distillation that converts pure AR model to DLLM with weaker performance but faster inference. Unlike prior work, we propose cross-paradigm OPD to jointly distill knowledge from strong AR VLM teacher and an image diffusion generation teacher into unified DLLM. Main Results Setup. We train NLD-Uni in three-stage manner. The first stage primarily includes text-image pairs for basic visual alignment and image generation capabilities. The second stage introduces additional data for instruction following, image editing, object grounding, and interleaved generation. The final stage is the unified OPD training stage, with Nemotron-3 Nano Omni as the teacher for multimodal reasoning tasks and Qwen-Image for image editing tasks. We also mix T2I SFT batches to preserve the text-to-image generation performance. Notably, we do not include an OPD teacher for T2I tasks because the base models performance on GenEval and HPSv3 is stronger than teacher candidates like Qwen-Image and Flux. The training is conducted on 64 H100 GPUs over 26 days. In particular, the final OPD stage takes 5 days. We defer additional details to Appendix B. Generic Understanding Tasks. We report the performance of image understanding tasks in Table 1. NLD-Uni outperforms the previous state-of-the-art unified diffusion model and diffusion VLMs like LLaDa-V [41], NLD-VLM [35] and LaViDa-O [11] by considerable margin on wide range of benchmarks such as MMMU [42], ChartQA [43], InfoVQA [44] and AI2D[45]. On object grounding benchmark RefCOCO [46] and GUI grounding benchmark ScreenSpot-Pro [47], NLD-Uni also demonstrates strong performance while most unified models are not equipped with this ability, unlocking new potential applications for diffusion language models. Conclusion Diffusion language models have attracted considerable attention in recent years for their greater efficiency compared with autoregressive models and their unified interface for multimodal data. However, their performance in practice still lags behind that of state-of-the-art models, limiting their adoption. In this paper, we propose two methods for developing more capable DLLMs: cross-paradigm on-policy distillation, which transfers knowledge from diverse teacher models, and self-refining diffusion process, which improves visual generation quality. Additional Related Works D.1. Unified Architecture. Unified MLLMs are capable of both understanding and generation tasks. Integrating different capabilities into single model presents unique architectural challenges. Generally, unified MLLMs have two common architecture choices. The first type, such as Janus [4], MMaDa [12], Show-O[64], uses single dense transformer to output both image and text tokens. The second type, such as BAGEL [5], MetaQueries [8] and LaViDa-O [11] employs separate parameter sets for handling image and text modalities. In particular, mixture-of-transformers (MoT) architecture [93] incorporates two separate sets of attention and FFN parameters to process different modalities, while still allowing cross-modal interaction via joint attention mechanism. Under this paradigm, several works such as X-Fusion and LM-Fusion [9, 94] further investigated architecture designs and training recipes of MoT. In particular, LaViDa-O [11] proposes Elastic-MoT design, which decouples the attention layer in the final half of the model and only enables joint attention in early layers. Given an 8B base model, Elastic-MoT extends it to 16B MoT. However, when performing understanding tasks, only 8B parameters are loaded. When performing generation tasks, only 8B generation parameters + 4B understanding parameters 32 Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-Uni: Elastic Self-Refining Unified Diffusion LLM with Cross-Paradigm On-Policy Distillation are loaded. When performing interleaved tasks, all 16B parameters are loaded. This elasticity makes the model particularly efficient and introduces no overhead compared to an 8B VLM when performing understanding tasks. E. List of Benchmarks . Multi-modal Reasoning: [100], [50], [101], DynaMath [102], Geometry3k [49], LogicVista [103], We-Math [48]. Multi-modal Generation: GenEval [59], DPG [60], HPSv3 [61], ImgEdit [65]. F. Limitations and Future Work In this work, we propose NLD-Uni, introducing self-refining diffusion process and cross-paradigm on-policy distillation. Despite considerable success, some limitations remain. First, while the cross-paradigm OPD framework allows us to distill an AR teacher to diffusion student, it still requires the vocabulary spaces of the two models to match. In our setup, both models use the Ministral 3 [104] tokenizer. Many existing works have explored cross-tokenizer distillation between AR models [105]. We leave extending these methods to support cross-paradigm distillation to future work. Second, while NLD-Uni achieves state-of-the-art performance among unified diffusion MLLMs, there may be considerable room for further optimization on the model architecture side. We leave that for future work as well since it is not the focus of this work. Third, we define the self-refining diffusion process with the non-Markov formulation with predefined per-token corruption intervals and uniform progression of intermediate states. This design is mostly motivated by minimizing complexity. Future work may explore defining Markov process with stochastic transition rate that allows tokens to stay at different intermediate states for varying lengths of time. Finally, from system perspective, NLD-Uni lacks fine-grained text rendering capabilities because such data is not widely present in the training mix. We will address this issue in future by curating additional text-rendering-focused data.
